items.bron: Wikipedia 'Strut' (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strut): a strut resists longitudinal compression; structural glossary cec.nic.in (Arch Paper35 glossary): strut = member subjected mainly to compression; RMIT Learning Lab, roof trusses p.4: compression members are struts. Volledig nagegaan in hierdie rondte.

items.bron: DBE 2023/24 ATP NST Gr 4: Term 1 contains the topic 'Structures for animal shelters' and Term 2 'Strong frame structures' lists 'Struts and frame structures' as its first core concept. Only the curriculum order is externally checkable; what Wolkskool's own earlier lessons say is outside a fact check.

items.bewering: 'n raamstruktuur is los dele wat aanmekaar sit met oop plekke tussen hulle. (Begrip: 'Los dele wat aanmekaar sit met oop plekke tussen hulle.')
items.blok: Stutte word aanmekaar gesit; begrip: raamstruktuur
items.bron: IALA Dictionary, 'Frame' (iala-aism.org): a group of component parts joined to provide strength and stability and to support loads; design/technology classification (frame vs solid vs shell): frames are separate members joined, with open spaces. Read alone the entry is true but leaves out that the parts hold up or carry something; that is incompleteness, not a falsehood.

items.bewering: Bouers sit baie stutte aanmekaar en maak so 'n raamstruktuur.
items.bron: Britannica 'truss' (britannica.com/print/article/607326): straight pieces joined into triangles; RMIT Learning Lab. Note: strictly, engineers call a pulled member a 'tie' and only a pushed member a 'strut'; calling every frame member a strut is CAPS's own naming ('stutte word verbind'). The lesson's later blocks wisely say 'dun dele' for real bridges, cranes and pylons, so no false claim results.

items.bewering: 'n Raam gee die maklikste mee by die plek waar twee stutte aanmekaar sit. Die twee stutte kan by daardie plek teen mekaar draai.
items.bron: WPI mathematics paper on rigidity (users.wpi.edu/~bservat/amsgeo.pdf): a pin-jointed four-bar frame changes shape with no bar changing length, i.e. only by turning at the joints; JoVE 'Frames': pin joints let members rotate freely. 'Die maklikste' holds for a frame of struts whose joints can turn, which is the frame the sentence describes.

items.bewering: Sit vier stutte in 'n vierkant aanmekaar. ... Die vierkant trek skeef en lyk nou soos 'n skuins ruit. Nie een van die vier stutte het langer of korter geword nie. Die stutte het net by hul verbindings gedraai, en die vorm het verander.
items.bron: Science Buddies, 'Popsicle Stick Trusses: What Shape Is Strongest?' (sciencebuddies.org): the square slides around while the triangle holds its shape; WPI rigidity paper: no SSSS theorem, so four side lengths do not fix a quadrilateral's shape. A square with equal sides racks into a rhombus ('skuins ruit').

items.bewering: Niks aan die driehoek se vorm verander nie. 'n Driehoek kan net van vorm verander as een van sy stutte langer of korter word. Elke stut is styf en bly net so lank as wat hy was.
items.bron: Britannica 'truss': a triangle cannot be distorted by stress; WPI rigidity paper: side lengths fix a triangle's angles, and it stays rigid as long as the rods and joints hold. Note on how this combines with the begrip 'stut': pushing sideways on the top corner pushes one sloping side and PULLS the other, so the triangle stays rigid only because a member also resists getting longer. The begrip defines a stut only by pushing from its ends. The lesson's sentence 'langer of korter' covers both, so nothing false is taught; a person may want the begrip read alongside it.

items.bewering: Bouers sit daarom driehoeke in 'n raam om hom sterk en stabiel te hou.
items.bron: Britannica 'truss'; Science Buddies trusses activity; truss sources: a truss is a series of triangles that keeps its shape under load.

items.bewering: 'n Dakkap is die raam van dun dele wat 'n dak dra. (Begrip: 'Die raam van dun dele wat binne 'n dak sit en die dak dra.')
items.bron: Franco Frescura architectural glossary on SAHO (francofrescura.sahistory.org.za/glossary/glossary-d/): DAKKAP = ROOF TRUSS; treeterms.co.uk 'roof truss': triangulated lattice of timbers designed to support a pitched roof.

items.bron: encyclopedia.com 'truss' and roof-truss sources: a truss carries the roof across the gap between the walls and spreads the weight to the walls; the covering rests on purlins/battens laid across the trusses, i.e. on top of them.

items.bron: Crane industry guides (almarwan.com lattice vs telescopic boom; fridayparts.com): cranes lift hook loads with a long boom/jib; Britannica 'truss' names cranes among truss uses. 'Hoë' is a fair description of the cranes a learner sees (tower and boom cranes).

items.bron: almarwan.com 'Lattice Boom vs Telescopic Boom': a lattice boom is an open truss giving high stiffness and strength with less dead weight than a similarly strong solid boom.

items.bewering: Ander hyskrane se arm lyk soos een dik balk sonder driehoeke.
items.bron: Dealer guide and patent US9908751B2 (patents.google.com): telescopic booms are box-section booms that extend within themselves.

items.bewering: 'n Kragmas is 'n hoë mas wat die kragdrade hoog bo die grond oor die land dra. Baie kragmaste is 'n staalraam van dun dele in driehoeke van die grond af tot heel bo. (Begrip: ''n Hoë mas wat kragdrade hoog bo die grond dra.')
items.bron: NWU Institutional Repository (repository.nwu.ac.za/handle/10394/19340): Eskom lines use galvanised lattice steel structures; Engineering News 2014-05-23 on Eskom towers; lattice-tower patents (USPTO 6745539): triangulated bracing between the legs over the height of the tower. 'Baie' is correct: Eskom also uses guyed V and cross-rope towers.

items.bewering: 'n Geraamte is die raam binne-in die lyf van 'n dier met 'n ruggraat.
items.bron: Sources conflict on the scope of the word. Biology: Britannica 'skeleton' (britannica.com/science/skeleton) defines a skeleton as the supportive framework of an animal body and says invertebrate skeletons may be external or internal (crabs, insects, sea urchins); San Diego Zoo glossary: an exoskeleton is a skeleton. Everyday dictionary sense: 'geraamte' = the bones of a person or animal in their natural arrangement (Weiland via DBNL; vocabulary.com nl 'geraamte': bones and cartilage), and only backboned animals have bone. Written as 'n Geraamte IS ...', the sentence defines the word, so under the biological sense it teaches that a beetle or crab has no skeleton. A person must decide which sense the subject uses, possibly subject-wide. A form true under both senses: 'By 'n dier met 'n ruggraat is die geraamte die raam binne-in sy lyf.'

items.bewering: Begrip geraamte: 'Die raam binne-in die lyf van 'n dier met 'n ruggraat, wat hom ophou.'
items.bron: Same conflict as the study sentence, and sharper here, because a glossary entry is read alone with no lesson around it: Britannica 'skeleton' (invertebrate skeletons, external or internal) against the everyday sense of 'geraamte' as the bones of an animal (Weiland/DBNL; vocabulary.com nl). Read alone, the entry says animals without a backbone have no skeleton. 'Wat hom ophou' is fine as 'supports him'. A person decides; a form true under both senses: 'By 'n dier met 'n ruggraat: die raam binne-in die lyf wat hom ophou.'

items.bewering: Die lang, harde dele binne 'n dier se pote werk soos stutte. Hulle dra die dier se gewig en hou hom op sy pote.
items.bron: CAPS's own statement in the kaps_punt ('ledemaatbene is stutte'); weight passes down the limb bones from joint to joint. Limit of the mapping: Biewener, 'Musculoskeletal design in relation to body size' (biewenerlab.oeb.harvard.edu) and Main & Biewener 2004 show that midshaft stresses in most long bones come mainly from BENDING, not pure end-on compression. Combined with the begrip 'stut' ('dra die gewig sonder om te buig'), the learner gets an idealised picture, but bones do not visibly bend, so a Grade 4 learner does not end up anywhere false.

items.bewering: Die stutte kom by gewrigte bymekaar en kan by daardie plekke draai.
items.bron: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 9.5 Synovial Joints (med.libretexts.org): the limb's joints (hip, knee, ankle, shoulder, elbow) are synovial joints that allow movement, including hinge and ball-and-socket rotation.

items.bewering: Sterk bande hou die stutte by die gewrigte saam
items.bron: Human Anatomy (OERI) 8.5 Synovial Joints (med.libretexts.org): ligaments hold the bones together and resist excess or abnormal motion.

items.bewering: spiere keer dat 'n gewrig vou.
items.bron: Harvard Health, 'Knee buckling raises the risk of falls' (health.harvard.edu): weak quadriceps go with knees buckling, and strengthening them improves knee stability; antigravity-muscle descriptions: the quadriceps keep the knee extended so the legs do not buckle, and the back extensors stop the trunk folding forward. Passive structures help in quiet standing, but the sentence does not say muscles are the only thing.

items.bewering: Analogie: stutte wat in 'n raam by hul verbindings draai, teenoor bene wat by gewrigte draai, met bande wat hulle saamhou en spiere wat keer dat die gewrig vou.
items.blok: Stutte word aanmekaar gesit; Druk teen 'n vierkant; Die geraamte
items.bron: Mapping checked against OpenStax/OERI joints, the frame-rigidity sources (WPI, Science Buddies, Britannica 'truss') and Biewener. Where a learner reasoning further ends up: a leg is a chain of struts that can turn at joints, so like the square it would fold under weight. The lesson then says correctly that ligaments only hold the joint together and muscles stop the fold. That holds and even matches the lesson's own rule, because a muscle across a joint acts as an adjustable third side and the bones turn only when it gets shorter or longer. The block does NOT claim the skeleton is built of triangles, which would be false for a limb. The only stretch is 'bones carry load end-on like struts' (they mainly carry bending, Biewener), which is below what a Grade 4 learner reasons with. No false destination found.

items.bewering: Begrip stut: ''n Lang, dun, stywe deel wat 'n gewig dra wanneer daar van sy twee ente af op hom gedruk word.'
items.bron: Wikipedia 'Strut'; cec.nic.in structural glossary; RMIT Learning Lab (strut = compression member). Read alone, true. Combined with the other entries: with 'geraamte'/'gewrig' (leg bones pushed from both ends by body and ground) it holds; with the triangle block, see the note there about the pulled side.

items.bewering: Begrip gewrig: 'Die plek waar dele van 'n geraamte bymekaarkom. By die meeste gewrigte kan hulle draai.'
items.bron: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 9.5 (med.libretexts.org): synovial (freely movable) joints are the most common type of joint in the body; fibrous joints such as skull sutures do not move. 'Die meeste' therefore holds.

items.bewering: Begrip stabiel: 'Iets is stabiel as dit sy vorm hou en bly staan wanneer jy daarteen druk.'
items.bron: Dictionary.com 'stable': of a structure, not likely to fall or give way; physics sense, reacts to a disturbing force by keeping or regaining position and form. YourDictionary (Webster's New World): not likely to break down, fall apart or give way.

opsomming: Every engineering and anatomy claim checks out, and the frame-to-skeleton comparison holds (muscles stopping a joint from folding fits the lesson's own triangle rule), but the definition of 'geraamte' in both the study text and the glossary says a skeleton IS the frame inside an animal with a backbone, and sources conflict on that scope: biology counts the shells of crabs and insects as skeletons, while the everyday sense of 'geraamte' means bones, so a person must decide the scope, possibly for the whole subject; a form true under both senses is 'By 'n dier met 'n ruggraat is die geraamte die raam binne-in sy lyf'.
